author: Mozart
title: The trials
where: *The Magic Flute*, Act 2: the questions before the trials, the Queen of the Night’s aria, and the end of the opera
about: Tamino, a prince, and Papageno, a bird-catcher, are at the priest Sarastro’s temple, where Tamino hopes to win Pamina, daughter of the Queen of the Night. In the first passage, which is spoken, two priests question them before their trials; Tamino has just said he seeks friendship and love. In the second the Queen has shown Pamina a dagger, told her to kill Sarastro and forbidden her to answer. In the third Papageno and his bride sing of the children they want, and a chorus of priests ends the opera.

view.says: Auden calls the opera overoptimistic. Tamino stands for the spiritual and gains wisdom and Pamina because he has the courage to stake his life in the trials. Papageno stands for the natural and is given Papagena because he has the humility to refuse the risk. The opera holds, he says, that nature and spirit can live together in man if each keeps to itself and the natural may refuse interference.
view.quote: he has had the humility to refuse to risk his life even if the refusal will mean that he must remain single
view.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 134–35

lenses.label: Word
lenses.caption: English stands under each phrase. Both men are asked with the same verb, erkämpfen, to win by fighting. Adelung’s dictionary of 1793 gives it to the higher style; its first example is winning a Sieg, victory: Tamino’s word. He calls Pamina holde, lovely, a word of the noble style. From the priest’s word Papageno takes the verb inside it, Kämpfen, and refuses it. He calls himself a Natursmensch, a man of nature; Auden says he stands for the natural. The bird-catcher hopes to catch, fange, a Weibchen: a wife in familiar speech, and the female of any animal. His last word here is ledig, single: what Auden says the refusal may cost him.
lenses.why: One high word asks two men whether they will win by fighting; Tamino takes it up and names his victory and reward, and Papageno refuses it in a bird-catcher’s familiar words: for Auden, the spiritual and the natural.

notes.gloss: Even if death were your lot?
notes.note: *Loos* is the lot drawn to settle a thing by chance; in the higher style, Adelung says, it is any fate a person does not owe directly to himself. An English version that Auden quotes in 1943 has *Fate* here.

notes.gloss: there is still time to withdraw

notes.note: *Hold*, in Adelung, is lovable, pleasing in a marked degree: a sense he gives to the noble style.
*Lohn* is the good done to a person for what he has done; the word returns in the last two lines of the opera, with the verb for winning and the word for wisdom.

notes.gloss: You will take on every trial?
I am a man of nature,
notes.note: Adelung, who spells the word *Naturmensch*, defines it as a person living in the state of nature, without any civil order or restraint from outside.

notes.gloss: who with sleep, food and drink

notes.note: In Adelung *Weibchen* is the more usual word for a married woman in familiar speech and the word for the female of any animal, the cock’s and the sparrow’s among his examples; Papageno says it again in the duet.
*Fangen*, in Adelung, is to get birds, fish or mice into one’s power by cunning and with tools such as a net, and in his first song Papageno wishes for a net to catch girls.

notes.gloss: What does this trial consist in?
To submit to all our laws,

lenses.stands: The marks on the two exchanges. The German words: Adelung’s dictionary of 1793 to 1801 under *Erkämpfen*, *Kämpfen*, *Los*, *Hold*, *Lohn*, *Sache*, *Naturmensch*, *Weib*, *Fangen* and *Ledig*, and under the other words glossed. Papageno’s trade and his net for girls: [his first song](#/read/magic-flute/act-1:35) in Act 1. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 134; the English version he quotes in 1943 is in *Auden Studies 3*, p. 15.

lenses.label: Answers
lenses.caption: Matching numbers mark where the second exchange answers the first. The priests set one test in the same words: erkämpfen, to win by fighting, and Tod, death, as the risk. Here Tamino is asked three questions and answers each in one word. Papageno gives his reasons, asks what the trial is, and at the word for death says he stays single. Auden and Chester Kallman, who put the opera into English, write that this exchange is Papageno’s trial, handled so lightly in the original that audiences can miss it. He passes, they say: his last answer shows his humility, and for it he is rewarded. Tamino, Auden says, is rewarded for the courage to stake his life.
lenses.why: The same test in the same words gets three one-word assents from Tamino and a refusal from Papageno; Auden holds that the opera rewards both, one for courage and the other for the humility of refusing.

ties.say: The same verb is put to both: to win by fighting.
Death is named to each: to Tamino as his possible lot, to Papageno as a thing he must not shun.
Asked about death, Tamino says yes. Told of it, Papageno says he stays single.
Tamino asks for wisdom’s teaching as his victory. Papageno wants no wisdom at all.
Tamino names Pamina as his reward. Papageno names no one: he hopes to catch a pretty little wife. Auden notes in 1946 that he is in love with no one woman: a girl is all he wants.
Tamino takes on every trial without asking what it is. Papageno asks.

lenses.stands: The marks on the two exchanges, and a count of the questions put to Tamino here and of the words in his answers. Papageno’s trial: Auden and Kallman, Preface to *The Magic Flute* (1956), in *Libretti and Other Dramatic Writings*, p. 132. Tamino’s reward: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 134. Papageno and a girl: “Mozart and the Middlebrow” (1946), in *Prose*, vol. II, p. 290.

lenses.label: Wishes
lenses.caption: Tamino’s answer to the warning is one sentence in two matched halves. Each names a thing he wants and calls it a prize: wisdom’s teaching is to be his Sieg, victory, and Pamina his Lohn, reward. The verb sey, be, is said once for both, a figure called zeugma. Auden says Tamino faces the ordeal knowing what lies beyond it: wisdom and the princess. Papageno begins with two refusals and puts his wish last, under an if. The priest answers nie, never, with a condition of his own, which Auden and Kallman call a threat. The opera does not carry it out: Papageno promises only silence and breaks it, never enters fire or water, and is given Papagena.
lenses.why: Tamino’s balanced sentence names wisdom and Pamina as his victory and reward, as Auden’s Tamino knows what waits beyond the ordeal; Papageno hangs his one wish on an if, and the priest’s threat of never is not carried out.
lenses.stands: The marks on the two speeches, and zeugma as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. Auden on Tamino: *The Enchafèd Flood*, p. 111. The priest’s threat, and the silence Papageno vows and does not keep: Auden and Kallman, Preface to *The Magic Flute* (1956), p. 132. Later in Act 2 Tamino and Pamina go [through fire and water](#/read/magic-flute/act-2:297) without Papageno, and [Papagena is brought to him](#/read/magic-flute/act-2:330).

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: five beats, the line beginning off the beat, in lines of eleven and ten syllables by turns
lenses.caption: The German has five beats to the line. Without rhyme, the line of five beats is the classic line of German verse drama since Lessing’s Nathan der Weise of 1779. Most of this libretto’s verse has four beats. The Queen has ten lines of five, these and two in Act 1; a chorus of priests, two armed men and three boys sing all the others. Auden and Chester Kallman, writing on the translation of opera, hold that the Queen, a supernatural being, cannot speak like a courtesan such as Verdi’s Violetta. The last line, to the gods, is broken twice and can be heard to begin on two stresses.
lenses.why: In this libretto lines of five beats go only to the Queen and to groups, which sets these lines apart from every other single character’s; Auden and Kallman hold that a supernatural being cannot be given a courtesan’s speech.

points.say: This line begins on a stressed word, *Tod*, death, where the measure has no beat.

As Mozart set them, the fifth and sixth lines become four short ones: the phrase meaning for ever is sung three times, once each with the words for cast off, forsaken and shattered. Auden and Kallman remark of Mozart in general that when a text is too short for his music he has its lines sung again.

The line turns from Pamina to the gods. Two dashes break it, and its first word, a command, can be heard as a stress before the beat. The libretto of 1791 prints *Rache*, vengeance, and *Götter*, gods, apart; as Mozart set them they are one word, *Rachegötter*, gods of vengeance.

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, with German Wikipedia on the five-beat line (“Blankvers,” “Jambischer Fünfheber”) and on this aria for the libretto’s usual four beats. A count of the five-beat lines in the libretto as printed in 1791. The English lines: the English libretto [printed here](#/read/magic-flute/act-2:45). Mozart’s text: the Mozarteum’s Libretti-Edition. Auden and Kallman: *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 490–91; Violetta is the heroine of [*La Traviata*](#/traviata).

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: Each set of four lines rhymes by turns, on two syllables in the odd lines and on one in the even, the usual way with this line in German. The two-syllable rhymes pair the Queen’s Herzen, heart, with Sarastro’s Todesschmerzen, pains of death, and the daughter verlassen, forsaken, with Sarastro erblassen, turning pale, a noble word for dying. The first set closes on nimmermehr, nevermore, and the second on Schwur, oath, which rhymes with Natur: she swears that nature’s bonds shall be shattered if Sarastro does not die by Pamina’s hand.
lenses.why: The two-syllable rhymes pair the Queen’s heart and her forsaken daughter with Sarastro’s dying; the sets close on nevermore and on oath, which rhymes with nature, whose bonds she swears shall be shattered.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage and what its lines say; after the aria Pamina says it is she who is to be cast off. Rhymes of two syllables and of one by turns: German Wikipedia, “Jambischer Fünfheber.” The German words: Adelung’s dictionary under *Erblassen*, *Verlassen*, *Nimmermehr*, *Schwur* and *Band*.

lenses.label: Threat
lenses.name: chiasmus
lenses.plain: a crossing: two things are named, then named again in the opposite order; here condition and penalty, then penalty and condition
lenses.caption: Five lines hold one threat, said twice in opposite order. The third line sets the condition, that Sarastro die at Pamina’s hand, and the fourth the penalty: she is a daughter no more. The fifth and sixth say the penalty again, and the seventh returns to the condition in four of the third line’s words, nicht durch dich Sarastro, not through you Sarastro. Condition, penalty, penalty, condition: a chiasmus, which shuts the penalty between two statements of the condition. Afterward Pamina asks the gods what to do; later she says her mother’s curse pursues her. Auden and Kallman list that curse among the sufferings she must learn to bear.
lenses.why: The condition is said at both ends and the penalty between; the lines leave Pamina the deed or the loss of her mother, and Auden and Kallman count her mother’s curse among the sufferings she must learn to bear.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and what the lines say. Chiasmus as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. Pamina’s account of the oath, her question to the gods and her words on her mother’s curse: the libretto of 1791, Act 2, Scenes 10 and 27; the English libretto has the question [here](#/read/magic-flute/act-2:55), without the gods. Auden and Kallman: Preface to *The Magic Flute* (1956), in *Libretti and Other Dramatic Writings*, p. 131.

lenses.label: English
lenses.caption: The English libretto names no translator. It keeps the five beats, two lines a syllable short, and at first the German word order: of hell the vengeance. It has none of the two-syllable rhymes: its first four lines do not rhyme, and its last four rhyme on one syllable. Auden and Chester Kallman, who translated the opera themselves, write that such rhymes are frequent in German and mostly comic in English, and that a solemn scene does better with no rhyme than with a laughable one. The English order differs too: as printed, the line set here under the seventh stands fifth, so that each condition comes before its penalty.
lenses.why: The English keeps the five beats and none of the two-syllable rhymes, which Auden and Kallman find mostly comic in English, and it puts each condition before its penalty, which undoes the crossing.

ties.say: The English has the German order: *hell* before *vengeance*.
The German line ends on a rhyme of two syllables. The English line ends on one syllable and has no rhyme.
*Bande der Natur* is kept word for word: *ties of nature*.
This line stands fifth in the English libretto, before the two lines of penalty.
*Erblassen* is to turn pale, a noble word for dying. The English says *dies* and adds *now*, which rhymes with *vow*.
The libretto of 1791 sets vengeance and gods apart with a comma and a dash. The English has one phrase, as Mozart’s setting has one word.

lenses.stands: The two versions as they stand, line under line, and a count of beats and rhymes in the English lines, which are [printed here](#/read/magic-flute/act-2:45) in their own order; the title page of that libretto names no translator. Auden and Kallman: *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 484 and 488. *Erblassen*: Adelung’s dictionary. Mozart’s text: the Mozarteum’s Libretti-Edition.

pair.label: The English libretto, each line under its German

plates.heading: The two rewards
plates.label: The Magic Flute: the duet, then the last chorus

lenses.label: Word
lenses.caption: Auden quotes these six lines from the opera’s end and sets Caliban’s three after them. Four are from the duet of Papageno and his bride; a chorus of priests sings the opera’s last two. The duet has Erst, first, and Dann, then; wieder, again; and the singers’ own names. The chorus’s two lines name no person: strength has won, and crowns beauty and wisdom with an ewiger, eternal, crown. Auden reads two rewards here: wisdom and Pamina for Tamino, who stands for the spiritual; Papagena for Papageno, who stands for the natural. Three of the chorus’s words stand in some form in Tamino’s sentence before the trials: victory, reward, wisdom.
lenses.why: The duet counts out children in words of order and the parents’ own names, and the chorus crowns beauty and wisdom for ever: Auden sets one song by the reward of the natural, the other by that of the spiritual.

notes.note: Adelung notes that *erst*, said of what comes first in time, is proper only to familiar speech.
*Wieder* means that a thing takes place anew, so that it must have taken place before.
*Siegte* is the verb of *Sieg*, victory, the word Tamino uses before his trials.
*Lohn*, reward, is Tamino’s other word before his trials: he asks for Pamina as his.

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The German words: Adelung’s dictionary under *Erst*, *Dann*, *Wieder*, *Klein*, *Siegen*, *Stärke*, *Krönen*, *Lohn*, *Schönheit*, *Weisheit* and *Ewig*. Who sings which lines: the libretto of 1791. Tamino’s sentence is in the first passage on this page. Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 134.

lenses.label: List
lenses.name: anaphora
lenses.plain: the same word at the head of line after line
lenses.caption: After a line that begins Erst, first, three begin Dann, then. One word at the head of line after line is called anaphora; it makes the lines a list, here of children. Each line ends in a name, his and hers by turns; the names differ by one letter, and each parent sings the lines that end in his or her own. The first two lines have the word for little, the next two wieder, again. A few lines on, in words Mozart did not set, the libretto has the parents, with the little ones at play round them, rejoice in their own image. Auden, in 1943, calls Papagena Papageno’s double, and says the two multiply at one with nature.
lenses.why: The repeated then makes the four lines a list of children named for their parents, a boy and a girl and the same again; Auden calls Papagena Papageno’s double and says the pair multiply at one with nature.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Anaphora as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. Who sings which line, the wish for children just before and the lines on the parents after: the libretto of 1791, with the Mozarteum’s Libretti-Edition for the lines Mozart did not set and Adelung’s dictionary under *Ebenbild*; the English libretto has [its own version of the duet](#/read/magic-flute/act-2:347). Auden: “Vocation and Society” (1943), in *Auden Studies 3*, p. 16.

lenses.label: Caliban
lenses.caption: Beside the duet are the three lines of Caliban that Auden prints after it. Prospero has charged Caliban with trying to rape his daughter. Caliban wishes it done: he would have peopled the island with Calibans. Auden finds one attitude in both: the pair are humble and innocent in it, Caliban guilty and defiant. The numbers mark what is shared and what is not. In both, children are to bear a parent’s name. The duet’s children are a gift hoped for from the gods, they come one at a time, and every second one bears the mother’s name. Caliban says I, and all his would bear his own.
lenses.why: Auden finds one attitude in the duet and in Caliban’s lines; both speak of children under their own names, which the pair hope for from the gods, one at a time, and Caliban would have made himself.

ties.say: The duet looks ahead, to a gift it hopes the gods will give. Caliban looks back on an act that Prospero prevented.
The child is to bear the father’s own name: a little Papageno, and Calibans.
Every second child in the duet bears the mother’s name. Caliban says *I*.
The duet counts one child at a time, and again. Caliban’s verb, *peopled*, speaks of a whole island at once.

lenses.stands: The marks on the two passages. Prospero’s charge: [*The Tempest*, Act 1, Scene 2](#/read/tempest/a1s2:198). The gift hoped for from the gods: the lines of the duet just before these in the libretto of 1791, and in the English libretto [here](#/read/magic-flute/act-2:347). Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 134; Caliban speaks again on [the page for *The Tempest*](#/tempest).

pair.label: The Tempest, Act 1, Scene 2: Caliban to Prospero

auden.says: He sets the opera beside *The Tempest*. (As a dictionary has it, the Manichees held matter to be evil; Pelagius denied original sin.) After the lines of the chorus and the duet he prints Caliban’s answer to Prospero. He likens Papageno’s refusal to a Caliban who thanks Prospero for his proposal to adopt and school him, and stays in the jungle. On the next page he sets the two men against Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, who act on each other; Tamino and Papageno do not.
auden.quote: If *The Tempest* is overpessimistic and manichean, *The Magic Flute* is overoptimistic and pelagian.
auden.source: “Balaam and His Ass,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 134–35

auden.says: A lecture of January 1943 opens with the questions of the first passage, in an English version. Tamino’s moral, he says there, is the familiar one: he is blessed for having staked everything, failure included. The surprise is that Papageno gets his girl too, because he is frankly and selfishly himself and would sooner give her up than die. Papagena, his double, is given him, and the two multiply at one with nature. But a Papageno who has been woken, he adds, cannot stay as he is: he must follow Tamino onward or sink to a Monostatos or a Caliban.
auden.source: “Vocation and Society” (1943), in *Auden Studies 3: “In Solitude, for Company”* (1995), pp. 15–16 and 18

auden.says: An essay of 1946 calls the story a parable about education with two heroes, a romantic one and a comic one. Tamino stakes his own life, and the princess with it, on the mere chance of marrying her. Papageno is in love with no one woman; a girl is all he wants. To be sure of his life he accepts staying single. He is rewarded all the same, and the pair expect to live on, not as themselves, in children without number. Tamino’s heroism, he says, is passion; Papageno’s is the humility to admit he has none.
auden.source: “Mozart and the Middlebrow” (1946), in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 290–91

auden.says: Lecturing on *The Tempest* in 1947, he says the play and the opera run parallel and ask the same thing, what education is. He pairs the persons: Sarastro with Prospero, the Queen of the Night with Sycorax, Monostatos with Caliban, Tamino and Pamina with Ferdinand and Miranda. Papageno, who refuses to be tested at the risk of death, still wins the prize, because he too will pay, in his own way: by staying single, or by taking an old woman for his wife.
auden.source: *Lectures on Shakespeare*, reconstructed and edited by Arthur Kirsch (2000), the lecture on *The Tempest*, p. 300

auden.says: In the preface to their English version, he and Chester Kallman find two themes in the story. One is a change in how Night stands to Day, instinct to reason: where the Queen and Sarastro were at war, Pamina and Tamino marry. The other is education: how someone finds his calling and what that asks of him. The story has two heroes, one needing courage to venture, one humility to stay at home; Papageno passes his trial when he chooses to stay single. The original blurs this, they say, keeping him on stage for laughs and having him vow a silence the audience knows he will break.
auden.source: W. H. Auden and Chester Kallman, Preface to *The Magic Flute* (1956), in *Libretti and Other Dramatic Writings by W. H. Auden, 1939–1973* (1993), pp. 129–32

auden.says: He and Kallman also wrote about the work of translating opera. *The Magic Flute*, they note, is made of separate musical numbers, and the talk between them is spoken. A libretto has two rhythms, the one its verse has when read aloud and the one the music gives it, and a translator must keep the second. Rhymes of two syllables, frequent in German, are mostly comic in English. And the style must suit the kind of opera and the kind of character.
auden.source: W. H. Auden and Chester Kallman, “Translating Opera Libretti,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 484–91

caveats: The preface of 1956 is by Auden and Chester Kallman together. That preface, the lecture of 1943 and the essay of 1946 were read here only in snippets of scanned copies, not in full.
Auden’s lecture of 1947 on *The Tempest* was put together by its editor from notes that students made, so its words may not be his; it too was read only in snippets.

Singers sing the aria as Mozart set it: words of the fifth and sixth lines come again, and *Rache* and *Götter* are one word. The lines shown are those of the libretto printed in 1791, so the record on this page will not match them word for word.

The English libretto printed here leaves out the spoken scene of the first passage, so the English under its phrases is this page’s own. Under the aria its lines are set in the German order; in that libretto the line shown seventh stands fifth.

The stresses marked in the aria are one reader’s: in three lines the fourth beat falls on a light word, and the last line’s first word can be heard lighter. The count of five-beat lines leaves out an irregular line of the two armed men and the duet’s stammered opening.
